source: General Directorate of Agriculture (GDA), Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, Cambodia — Sweet Corn Production Handbook (ផលិតកម្មដំណំពោតផ្អែម), in partnership with SNV
text:
Black Cutworm (ដង្កូវកាត់ដើម, Agrotis ipsilon): Symptoms — the base of the corn plant is completely eaten through, at or just below soil level, especially in newly emerged and young vegetative-stage plants. The cutworm cuts the plant off at the base, sometimes dragging cut stem pieces into its burrow to feed, and may also feed on roots. Prevention — avoid planting in fields with a history of cutworm damage; keep the field and surrounding area free of weeds for at least 2-3 weeks before planting to reduce cutworm buildup; plow and sun-dry the field well before planting to expose eggs and larvae to sunlight and natural predators such as birds; select resistant varieties; use light traps at night, placed away from the field. Control — hand-collect and destroy larvae in small fields; use pheromone traps placed near each plant base — cutworms emerging to feed fall into the trap and are caught there; use botanical/plant-extract pesticides where available; as a last resort, use chemical insecticides applied before planting and again in the evening before cutworms emerge, such as Fipronil or Diafenthiuron.

Army Worm (ដង្កូវហ្វូង / ដង្កូវទ័ព, Spodoptera sp.): Symptoms — when food runs out in one area, armyworms move in large groups (like an army) across the ground seeking new food sources; eggs are laid in dense clusters; in years of severe outbreak, armyworms can strip a field of crop entirely, very quickly. Prevention — burn/destroy old stalks and crop residue after harvest, and keep the field weed-free to reduce food and shelter that sustain armyworm populations, since they can hide in weeds near the field and continue attacking newly planted crops; plow and turn over soil at the start of the season and after harvest, exposing pupae to sunlight and predators such as birds; flood the field to drown pupae and other soil pests before preparing land for the next crop; select resistant varieties; use pheromone traps to catch adult moths, which helps suppress reproduction and forecast population levels. Control — hand-collect adults and egg masses and destroy them, or feed them to poultry/ducks (highly effective for small plots); use botanical pesticides where locally available; as a last resort, use chemical insecticides including Diafenthiuron, Methomyl, Permethrin, Cypermethrin, Carbaryl, Chlorpyrifos, and Lambda-cyhalothrin — always read and follow label instructions carefully.

Corn Earworm (ដង្កូវស៊ីស្រុះផ្លែពោត, Helicoverpa zea): Symptoms — larvae bore into the ear and feed on kernels from young larval stage to maturity; heavy infestation damages the ear and reduces yield. Control — cut off and remove damaged parts, or hand-pick larvae, burn and bury away from the field; plow soil deeply; use yellow sticky traps or light traps; use insecticides such as Chlorantraniliprole, Indoxacarb, Cypermethrin, and Fipronil.

Corn Borer (ដង្កូវស៊ីរងដើម, stem borer): Symptoms — this pest causes severe damage; larvae first feed on young leaves, then bore into the stem; heavy infestation can cause stalks to break in wind. Control — destroy pest habitat/host weeds in and around the field; collect and destroy egg masses, larvae, and pupae; use light traps or pheromone traps to catch adult moths.

Corn Flea Beetle (ទកគូពោត): Symptoms — feeding suppresses plant growth; causes small scattered holes/scarring on leaves; commonly found on stems and leaves, feeding especially in cool weather, hiding at the base of the plant during hot daytime conditions. Control — plow and sun-dry soil to kill eggs, larvae, and pupae, and flood before land preparation; rotate corn with other crops; use pheromone traps to attract and catch adults; heavy rainfall can also help control flea beetle populations by washing adults off leaves and preventing egg-laying in soil.
